newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH BUDGET TALKS SEEN MARKET-NEUTRAL -ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH BUDGET TALKS SEEN MARKET-NEUTRAL -ANALYSTS.

text.p: Finland is heading for tough talks next week on the 1998 budget amid political tensions triggered by new spending cut plans from the finance ministry, but financial markets are at ease, economists said on Friday.
The finance ministry in July proposed capping next year's state budget spending at 188 billion markka against 191 billion projected in June, and down from about 192 billion this year.
The budget deficit is proposed to be cut to 17 billion markka from an earlier planned 21 billion and from some 25 billion expected in 1997.

"I would be surprised if the government does not achieve this (new) goal," said Esko Torsti, chief analyst at SE-Banken in Helsinki. "And even if the budget swells to the earlier proposed 191 billion and the deficit to 21 billion the market reaction would be minor."
A forex dealer said he did not think the markka would react at all.

If the finance ministry's tightening plan succeeds, social democratic Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's five-party coalition will have two to three billion markka in leeway to trim taxes, economists said.
Income tax cuts could be a necessary sweetener in an incomes settlement for 1998, economists said.
"Even if tax cuts would deepen the deficit, the positive employment effects could balance the scales," a treasury manager said.
"Somewhat higher money market rates are the worst-case scenario," he added.
Long bonds would not react as long as the budget deficit remained around 20 billion markka, one analyst said.

But the Bank of Finland might hike short interest rates if it judged that fiscal policy was turning too lax, he said, referring to a deficit sliding back to over 20 billion markka from the now targetted 17 billion.
